stances.claim: Ressa's prescription defense is wobbly because she was charged under RA 10175 (Cybercrime Act), which prescribes in 12 years, not under the Revised Penal Code's ordinary libel (which prescribes in 1 year and the DOJ already conceded had prescribed for the 2012 original posting).
stances.rhetorical_move: statute-identification-as-defense-defeat (the wrong statute is being defended against)
stances.confidence: asserted with 'in my humble view' marker

stances.claim: Ressa's ex post facto defense is also not viable because the charge concerns the Feb 19, 2014 republication, which occurred when the Cybercrime Law was already in effect -- not the May 29, 2012 original posting which the DOJ explicitly exonerated.
stances.rhetorical_move: timing-analysis-with-illustrative-jaywalking-example (using a vivid pedagogical analogy to clarify the ex post facto doctrine)

stances.claim: Despite these defense weaknesses, Ressa has VIABLE defenses including: (a) the Rappler article was privileged as 'fair commentary on a matter of public interest' under Borjal v. CA (provided Keng's public-figure status can be established), (b) the inapplicability of the old RPC republication doctrine to new cyber libel, (c) equal protection violation via selective justice, and (d) lack of probable cause.
stances.rhetorical_move: defense-strength-redirection (rejecting the headlines defenses, identifying the actually viable ones)

stances.claim: The after-hours warrant service and overnight detention -- though deplorable -- will have minimal legal effect on Ressa's culpability for cyber libel; the appropriate remedy is administrative sanctions against the offending public officials, which the NBI is already investigating.
stances.rhetorical_move: procedural-vs-substantive distinction (irregularity in arrest does not absolve substantive liability)

notable_anecdotes: The DOJ's pedagogical clarity that 'the first publication of the article on 29 May 2012 is not covered by the Cybercrime Act of 2012, considering that the law was promulgated only in September 2012' -- used as the column's foundational date-line establishing what Ressa was NOT charged with.

Justice Secretary Guevarra's defiant public statement: he 'insisted he broke no law in filing the criminal charge and dared Ressa to sue him if she thought he violated her rights' -- capturing the tonal posture of the prosecution.

CJ's jaywalking illustration of ex post facto: 'A pedestrian crossed a street on Jan. 1, 2019. A month later, a new law was passed punishing that very act of jaywalking on Jan. 1' -- the most accessible pedagogical illustration of the doctrine in the column series.

The closing legal-realism caveat: 'perceived facts must be converted to legal facts by the lawyers of both sides via the rules of evidence; otherwise, courts cannot use them in their judgments' -- reminding readers that political narrative and legal proof are not the same.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban sets the record straight on the Maria Ressa cyber libel case: the DOJ in its January 10, 2019 Resolution explicitly exonerated her from libel for the original May 29, 2012 Rappler posting (because the Cybercrime Act was not promulgated until September 2012), and charged her and writer Reynaldo Santos Jr. only for the 'republication' of February 19, 2014 under the multiple publication rule articulated in Soriano v. IAC (November 9, 1988). Because the operative statute is RA 10175 (which prescribes in 12 years for cyber libel) rather than the Revised Penal Code's ordinary libel (which prescribes in 1 year), her prescription defense is 'wobbly.' Her ex post facto defense is similarly inviable because the charged act (the 2014 republication) occurred while the Cybercrime Law was already in effect -- CJ illustrates with a jaywalking analogy. He pivots to the defenses Ressa actually has: (a) the Rappler article may be privileged as 'fair commentary on a matter of public interest' under Borjal v. CA (January 14, 1999), provided that complainant Wilfredo Keng -- a private individual -- can be shown to have attained 'public figure' status; (b) the old RPC multiple-publication doctrine may not transpose to cyber libel; (c) selective justice may breach equal protection; and (d) probable cause itself may be absent. The deplorable after-hours warrant service and overnight detention, he says, will have minimal effect on substantive culpability though administrative sanctions against the agents are appropriate and the NBI is already investigating. He closes with the universal litigation caveat: 'perceived facts must be converted to legal facts by the lawyers of both sides via the rules of evidence; otherwise, courts cannot use them in their judgments.'
